description: Hi, we’re Team RAYNEX, a group of students led by Santhosh Dharshan S, a B.Tech Artificial Intelligence and Data Science student at Bannari Amman Institute of Technology, Sathyamangalam.
summary:
Field Intel: Know your field before the season changes

Field Intel is a free, mobile-first web app that turns NASA satellite and weather data into simple, timely advice for farmers. It tells them when to water, what to sow and when to act. Farming by the old calendar is becoming risky: monsoon rain is less predictable, heat at flowering is cutting yields, and fixed sowing dates no longer match the rain.

Field Intel compares a farmer’s last 90 days with 20 years of NASA records for the same place. It uses NASA POWER, SMAP soil moisture, GPM IMERG rainfall and MODIS crop health. It turns that comparison into a clear field status, up to three actions for the week, irrigation guidance and a printable 90-day plan. Alerts and an AI assistant that takes questions by text or voice support each step.

The app works in English, Hindi and Tamil, runs on low-cost phones, works offline, and needs no login. Farm details stay on the device. The demo uses real data from drought-prone Marathwada, India, so farmers can act on this season’s conditions rather than on an average year.
details:
Overview

Field Intel is a mobile-first decision-support platform. It turns NASA Earth observation data into clear, practical guidance for smallholder farmers. It addresses the core pressures named in the Field Shift challenge: shifting temperatures, changing rainfall, water scarcity and declining soil health. It does so by putting satellite data in a form farmers can act on.

Functionality

Users register a field by searching for their village or selecting it on a map, then outline its boundary. They add their crops, water source and main farming priority. No account is required, and all profile data stays on the user’s device. Field Intel then compares current conditions at the field with its long-term climate baseline and presents the results as:

A field status indicator: a three-level assessment (normal, caution, action required) shown with colour, an icon and a one-line summary, so it doesn’t rely on colour alone.

Weekly recommendations: up to three prioritised actions, including irrigation guidance.

Seasonal comparison: rainfall and temperature for the current season against historical normals.

Satellite field view: an interactive map with NASA layers for vegetation health, soil moisture and precipitation.

A 90-day crop plan: a week-by-week schedule built from crop growth stages and current weather, exportable as a PDF.

An alerts system: in-app notifications and push notifications for weather events and other risks.

An AI farm assistant: a conversational assistant that takes text or voice input, answers using the farmer’s own field data, and can read responses aloud. When a question needs expert diagnosis, it refers the user to the local Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK).

NASA data sources

Field Intel uses NASA POWER for daily precipitation and temperature records and for climate baselines from 2001 to 2025. SMAP provides soil moisture, GPM IMERG provides precipitation estimates, and MODIS provides NDVI vegetation health. The map layers stream from NASA GIBS. Locations outside the pre-loaded demonstration area are retrieved live from the NASA POWER API.

Benefits

Field Intel turns complex Earth observation data into a decision a farmer can make in seconds. The interface is fully available in English, Hindi and Tamil and avoids technical terms throughout. Offline support keeps the latest guidance available without a connection. Every figure shows its data source and observation date, and sample data is clearly labelled.

Intended impact

Our demonstration region is Marathwada, where agriculture depends almost entirely on the monsoon, making farmers highly vulnerable to drought and erratic rainfall. We added Punjab, a largely irrigated region, as a comparison. Better-timed sowing, irrigation and crop protection can help farmers conserve water, lower input costs and reduce crop losses, making farming more resilient to climate change.

Technology stack

The application is built in JavaScript, HTML and CSS using Vite. It is delivered as an installable Progressive Web App, with a service worker for offline access. Mapping uses Leaflet, Esri World Imagery, OpenStreetMap, Nominatim geocoding and NASA GIBS. The AI assistant runs on the Claude API from Anthropic, with Google Gemini as a fallback. It is served through a server-side function so that no API credentials reach the browser. The Web Speech API provides speech input and read-aloud in Indian English, Hindi and Tamil. Firebase Cloud Messaging delivers push notifications, and the platform is hosted on Vercel’s Mumbai region. Automated tests cover translations, the advice engine, climate calculations and map logic. No special hardware is required: the platform runs on low-cost Android phones.

Innovation

Most climate information tools present data in charts made for technical users. Field Intel turns the same data into a single status, a short explanation and a small set of actions. The AI assistant is grounded in each user’s own field data and speaks their language. The platform also states plainly when data is uncertain instead of presenting false precision, which builds trust with users.

Design considerations

The team designed for smallholder farmers who may have limited reading skills, use entry-level phones, work outdoors in bright light and have unreliable connectivity. Accessibility features include high contrast, adjustable text size, signals that don’t depend on colour, and voice interaction. On privacy and security, no login is required, user data stays on the device, API keys are kept on the server, and AI requests are rate-limited. The assistant also won’t generate prices, government scheme details or chemical dosages, so it never gives unverified advice.
